title: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation
hook: Most agent-optimization papers report a one-shot gain and stop. Rerun the optimizer on new tasks and two of three popular methods actually make the agent worse than doing nothing.
key_points: Tests whether agent-harness optimizers (GEPA, Meta Harness, RELAI-VCL) keep improving across two rounds of new tasks, not just one fixed benchmark.
All three beat the baseline in the standard single-phase setup — the gap only shows up once new tasks arrive.
GEPA's optimized agent transfers below the unoptimized baseline; Meta Harness transfers fine but stalls on the second round.
RELAI-VCL is the only method that transfers positively and keeps improving after folding new tasks into the objective.
Lifelong average pass rate on hard Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks: 76.4% (RELAI-VCL) vs. 66.0% (GEPA) vs. 64.6% (Meta Harness) vs. 58.7% (baseline).
The authors trace the difference to regression control built into the optimization loop, which discourages shortcut fixes that don't generalize.
content_html: Papers about agent-optimization methods usually report one number: how much better the agent got after being optimized against a fixed benchmark. That's not the situation a deployed agent actually faces, where optimization gets applied again and again as new failures and new tasks show up. This paper asks the harder question: do those gains actually stack up over multiple rounds, or do they erode?
extra_html:
Wenxiao Wang, Priyatham Kattakinda, and Soheil Feizi built a two-phase continual-learning evaluation from hard Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks and compared three agent-harness optimizers — GEPA, Meta Harness, and RELAI's Verifiable Continual Learning (RELAI-VCL) — under identical budgets. All three beat the baseline in the conventional single-phase test. But once a second batch of tasks arrived, they diverged sharply: GEPA's optimized agent fell below the unoptimized baseline, Meta Harness held its transfer gains but couldn't improve further, and only RELAI-VCL both transferred well and kept improving once the new tasks were folded into its objective, ending with the highest lifelong average pass rate (76.4% vs. 66.0%, 64.6%, and 58.7% for the others).

The authors attribute the split to regression control baked into RELAI-VCL's optimization loop — an inductive bias against shortcut fixes that happen to work on the current benchmark but don't generalize. Their takeaway for the field: agent-optimizer papers should report continual, not just one-shot, results, since a method's static-benchmark win says little about whether it survives repeated real-world updates.

related.title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench: Testing the Limits of Agents on Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks
related.hook: 46 terminal tasks that take hours, not minutes — and today's best agent still only nails 15% of them, with the average model managing barely 4%.

flashcards.prompt: Why isn't a single-round optimization gain enough evidence that an agent optimizer works?
flashcards.back_html: Deployed agents get optimized repeatedly as new tasks arrive. A method can win the standard one-shot benchmark and still fail to compound — or even regress — once a second round of optimization is applied.

flashcards.prompt: What happened to GEPA's optimized agent once new tasks were introduced?

choices.text: It transferred below the unoptimized baseline agent
It kept improving at the same rate as before
It matched RELAI-VCL's lifelong pass rate

flashcards.explanation_html: GEPA's gains didn't hold up: on the new tasks its optimized agent actually underperformed the plain, unoptimized baseline.

flashcards.prompt: What did the authors credit for RELAI-VCL being the only method that kept compounding?

choices.text: Regression control built into the optimization loop, discouraging shortcuts that don't generalize
Using a much larger optimization budget than the other methods
Training on Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks ahead of time

flashcards.explanation_html: All three methods used identical optimization budgets; RELAI-VCL's edge came from an inductive bias against shortcut solutions, not extra compute or data.
